content: Programs must establish which clinical and laboratory services are available at each level of the healthcare delivery system. Program managers should take into account the values and preferences of patients, the number of individuals likely to access decentralized settings, and whether decentralization reduces the need for patients to travel long distances to receive antiretroviral therapy (ART). Decentralization efforts should be supported by strengthening linkage and referral systems. Community-based treatment programs should be integrated with regular care at health facilities and supported by adequate laboratory services, diagnostics, monitoring, evaluation, and drug and supply management systems. Standards of care must be clearly defined for each level of the health system, ensuring that the roles of each level align with their capacity. Lines of authority and accountability should be explicit and well understood. In many settings, decentralizing ART requires task shifting to ensure an appropriate mix of healthcare workers at peripheral facilities. A suitable regulatory framework, including laws, regulations, policies, and guidelines, is necessary to allow tasks to be performed by different cadres of healthcare workers. Adaptations may be required for specific populations. HIV care and treatment services for pregnant and postpartum women, as well as HIV-exposed and infected children, can be effectively provided in decentralized settings. This approach is preferred in areas with a high HIV burden and where large numbers of women and children access primary care services. In low HIV burden settings, a centralized service delivery model with community linkages may be more appropriate. Certain groups, such as adolescents and key populations, may prefer to receive HIV services at facilities farther from their homes due to concerns about stigma and disclosure. In such cases, program managers should incorporate client values and preferences into the design of service delivery models. Chronic care requires the integration and linkage of related services to ensure comprehensive and consistent patient management over time. This includes providing related services in the same settings, establishing systems for information sharing, and ensuring effective referrals across settings and providers. Integrating and linking services can reduce missed opportunities for initiating ART, enhance adherence support, and optimize retention in care. In generalized epidemic settings, ART should be initiated and maintained for eligible pregnant and postpartum women and infants in maternal and child healthcare settings. These settings should be linked to ongoing HIV care and ART services where appropriate. All individuals living with HIV are now eligible to initiate ART regardless of CD4 cell count. Maternal and child health settings provide a critical opportunity to offer ART, as many women living with HIV access healthcare only during pregnancy. In most generalized HIV epidemic settings, maternal and child health services are delivered at the primary care level, where pregnant women and children predominantly access care. WHO recommends couple and partner HIV testing for all pregnant women and their partners in maternal and child healthcare services in generalized HIV epidemics. Such testing should also be considered for key populations in concentrated and low-level epidemics. ART should be available in maternal and child health clinics or easily accessible through linked service delivery models. Countries with generalized epidemics may adopt a phased approach to providing ART in maternal and child health settings, prioritizing facilities with the highest HIV burden and building health systems to ensure uninterrupted ART, adherence, and retention. Not all maternal and child health settings will have the capacity to provide long-term HIV treatment and care for women, their partners, and children. These settings must assess the optimal timing for transitioning and linking mothers and their infants to chronic HIV care. Factors to consider include the capacity and quality of HIV care in maternal and child health settings, the acceptability and proximity of alternative HIV care settings, and the local HIV burden. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated for people living with HIV in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. Similarly, TB treatment may be provided for people living with HIV in HIV care settings where a TB diagnosis has been made. These recommendations aim to expand ART coverage for people living with HIV and TB and support the diagnosis and treatment of active TB. Infection control measures are crucial in HIV care settings to minimize the risk of nosocomial TB transmission. ART should also be initiated and maintained for eligible individuals living with HIV in care settings where opioid substitution therapy (OST) is provided. OST, combined with psychosocial support, is recommended for treating opioid dependence. Where available, OST should be integrated and administered alongside ART for those in need. However, OST should not be a prerequisite for initiating or maintaining ART for people who use opioids. Efforts should be made to ensure ART is available as part of prison health services, given the high incarceration rates among people who inject drugs. Continuity of treatment and care must be maintained through appropriate referrals when individuals return to the community. Sexually transmitted infection (STI) and family planning services can be integrated within HIV care settings. There is significant overlap in the demographics and risk profiles of individuals accessing HIV treatment and care services and those accessing sexual and reproductive health services. Routine HIV testing should be offered to individuals with an STI in all epidemic settings and to family planning clients in generalized epidemic settings. Integration of these services can expand access and improve outcomes, particularly for women living with HIV who often have high rates of unintended pregnancy and unmet family planning needs. Adolescent-friendly family planning services should be prioritized for young women, who are more likely to experience unintentional pregnancies and higher mother-to-child transmission rates compared to adult mothers. Integrated service delivery is cost-effective and leads to economies of scale. It also improves access and expands opportunities to provide STI and family planning services to key populations, including adults and adolescents. The dual elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis is a global public health objective, and integrating syphilis diagnosis with HIV testing services is increasingly common.
